newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan may ban utility investment in China.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan may ban utility investment in China.

text.p: Taiwan said on Thursday it may ban firms from investing in utilities and public works in rival China -- a squeeze that would finalise a stay on conglomerate Formosa Plastics' US$3 billion-power plant project.
"We have asked scholars and experts to draft a set of new criteria for local investment in mainland China," Teng Sung-tang, a section chief of the economics ministry, told Reuters by telephone.
"Under the criteria, investment on such utilities as power plants, as well as public work projects, including railway and highway, would be barred," said Teng.
Taiwan bans direct investment in China but allows a wide range of projects routed through a third place.

An official from Formosa, Taiwan's biggest industrial conglomerate, told Reuters by telephone that the new tightening proposal was aimed specifically at scuttling his company's thermal power plant project in Zhangzhou, southern China.

"Under the cautious government policy, it would not come as a surprise to us if the government decides to adopt new criteria to specifically ban power plant investment in mainland China," the official, who declined to be named.

Taipei recently forced Formosa to suspend its project due to concerns that the island's economy was becoming too dependent on its political arch rival. But Formosa chairman Wang Yung-ching said his group would not abandon the China project even if it meant waiting for "six months or one year".
Taiwan's Investment Commission denied the government was targeting Formosa in the proposal.

"Wang Yung-ching had already given his word that he would not proceed on his Zhangzhou project as long as the government did not approve it," Tsai Lien-sheng, executive secretary of the commission, told state-funded Central News Agency.
He said the government would seek consensus from leading businessmen and industralists before adopting the new criteria.
Some 30,000 Taiwan businesses have poured an estimated US$30 billion worth of investments into China via a third area since a cross-strait political thaw began in the late 1980s.
But last week, economics minister Wang Chih-kang said Taipei would not further loosen economic links with the mainland unless Beijing eased its "hostility" against Taiwan.

Beijing, which suspected that Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui was supporting an independence movement on the island, staged a series of war games from August 1995 to March 1996 to try to intimidate the island.
China has viewed Taiwan as a renegade province since the two split after a civil war in 1949. Beijing has threatened to attack if Taipei tries to declare independence.
